analysis.one_liner: Tightens Superfund toxic-site cleanups to protect children's health, funded by reinstated polluter-pays taxes.
analysis.headline: The Superfund cleanup bill had 62 House backers but never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have reauthorized the Superfund law that cleans up the nation's worst toxic waste sites, with new rules putting children's health first: cleanups would have to reach background contamination levels unless a weaker standard was proven safe for kids. It would have given communities near contaminated sites money for independent experts, a formal advisory group on demand, health services, and fast-tracked cleanups in low-income areas, while making federal agencies follow the same cleanup rules as everyone else. To pay for it, the bill would have reinstated Superfund excise taxes on chemical and petroleum companies through 2003.
analysis.who_benefits: Families living near Superfund sites, especially children and residents of low-income or minority communities that host contamination, would get stricter cleanups, health assessments and services for affected communities, full replacement value if their home had to be bought out, and a real seat at the table through advisory groups and technical-assistance grants. Local governments would get brownfield cleanup and job-training grants, and workers could be trained for cleanup jobs in their own communities.

how_it_helps.text: Makes children's health the default cleanup standard: unless a risk-based standard is proven safe for children, remediation must reduce contamination to background levels to the maximum extent technically feasible, and judges remedies partly on protection of fetuses, children, and other highly susceptible groups.

Gives affected communities real leverage: technical assistance grants of up to $100,000 to hire their own experts, a Community Advisory Group that just 10 residents can trigger (whose consensus land-use recommendation the government must adopt), and state Community Information and Access Offices funded at $500,000 to $1,000,000 a year.

Directs health agencies to assess every Superfund site, provide health services to affected communities for fiscal years 2000-2004, notify local health officials of releases, and pay relocated residents the full replacement value of their homes.

Creates an environmental-justice fast track: facilities in economically distressed or socially disenfranchised areas get deadlines for assessment and listing, and their cleanups must be completed within three years of landing on the national priorities list.
Ends the federal government's special treatment: federal agencies would follow the same cleanup rules as private parties, with sovereign immunity waived and penalties enforceable against them.

Expands the public's right to know what is in their neighborhood: annual disclosure by responsible parties of hazardous substance quantities and potential worker exposure, plus first-time reporting on 'unstudied' chemicals whose toxicity has never been assessed.
Keeps cleanup funded by polluters rather than general taxpayers by extending the Superfund excise taxes on chemical and petroleum feedstocks through fiscal year 2003.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical and petroleum manufacturers would pay reinstated Superfund excise taxes through 2003; parties responsible for contamination would fund site-specific cleanup guarantees, face punitive damages of up to twice cleanup costs for willful releases, and make annual disclosures; federal agencies would lose their liability immunity. Some of the tax cost could reach consumers through product prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chemical, oil, and other polluting companies

drawbacks.text: Reinstating the Superfund excise taxes on chemical and petroleum feedstocks raises business costs that can be passed into the prices of everyday goods, and the bill also increases penalty ceilings under Superfund.

The default requirement to clean up to background contamination levels — unless the government affirmatively proves a weaker standard is safe for children — is stricter than current practice and could sharply raise the cost of some cleanups, potentially slowing the reuse of contaminated land even as the bill's brownfield grants try to speed it up.

Sites where contamination is left above unrestricted-use levels would need a dedicated fund paid into by responsible parties, a significant new financial obligation layered on top of the existing liability system.

While adding punitive damages for willful releases, the bill also exempts small waste contributors and municipal solid waste handlers from liability and eases liability for prospective purchasers, which critics of any liability relief argue can dilute the polluter-pays principle the same bill otherwise strengthens.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For communities living with toxic sites, the benefits were substantial and concrete: stricter cleanups keyed to children's health, health services, relocation payments, community advisory power, and a fast track for distressed neighborhoods. The main costs fall on chemical, petroleum, and waste-handling companies through reinstated taxes, liability, and new disclosure — with some pass-through to consumers — and the background-level cleanup default could make some remediation expensive. On balance the design is strongly pro-community, and it even includes business-friendly brownfield liability relief and small-party exemptions that temper the burden; its fatal weakness was political, not structural.

outcome.mechanism: Sent to three House committees the day it was introduced, it never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; a June 1998 entry pointed to a separate Superfund bill instead, and it died when the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on February 25, 1998 with a long list of original cosponsors, describing it as a reauthorization of the Superfund hazardous waste law.
Support grew to 61 cosponsors — 60 Democrats and 1 Independent — with no Republican backers.

The House referred it to three committees (Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Ways and Means) on the day of introduction, and in March 1998 it was sent to subcommittees in Commerce and Transportation; no committee ever reported it out.
On June 9, 1998, the action history records only a cross-reference to H.R. 2727, a separate Superfund bill the House pursued instead; H.R. 3262 itself never advanced further.
The bill received no vote in either chamber and expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical, petroleum, and nuclear companies that would have paid the reinstated Superfund taxes and faced stricter cleanup standards and disclosures are better off because the bill never advanced. The House Republican majority, which instead pursued its own Superfund bill, also got the outcome it wanted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Polluting industries that avoided reinstated taxes and stricter cleanups

sides.party_line_note: All 61 cosponsors were Democrats plus one Independent, with no Republican support, and the bill died in committees controlled by the Republican majority.

industries.note: Would pay extended Superfund excise taxes, face first-time reporting on unstudied chemicals, and remain liable for strict child-protective cleanups. Its interest in weaker cleanup and no new taxes ran against communities living with contamination.
The bill extends Superfund's environmental income tax and financing rate to taxable years through 2003, a direct cost to petroleum feedstock producers.

industries.industry: Hazardous waste generators and site owners (potentially responsible parties)
industries.note: New site-specific cleanup funds, punitive damages up to twice cleanup costs, and public disclosure cut against them, but the bill also grants liability exemptions for small contributors, municipal solid waste, and bona fide prospective purchasers. The core thrust is more liability, not less.

The bill declares the NRC's 1997 site-decontamination regulations not sufficiently protective, tightens rules for radioactively contaminated sites, and makes uranium dioxide a taxable chemical when used as reactor fuel.

industries.industry: Federal government as property owner and polluter
industries.note: Federal agencies would lose sovereign immunity and face the same cleanup rules, penalties, and deed assurances as private parties, protecting neighbors of military and Energy Department sites.

Stricter cleanups, institutional control registries, brownfield assessments, and worker-training grants would expand demand for cleanup, assessment, and monitoring work, including jobs recruited from affected communities.
Liability relief for innocent landowners and prospective purchasers, plus EPA and HUD brownfield grants and revolving loan funds, would make reusing abandoned industrial land easier and cheaper.
